ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Restore EBITDA margin toward 10% and protect program profitability across the remaining multi-year backlog, while setting disciplined pricing for the next bid cycle. CEO must decide within ~120 days whether to file Requests for Equitable Adjustment (REAs) and how to price upcoming FFP bids before the re-pricing window closes.
ownerConstraints: Contractual constraint: Firm-fixed-price multi-year contracts cannot be reopened unilaterally. Price relief requires negotiated change orders, REAs, or contractually grounded claims; unilateral price increases would constitute breach.

Regulatory constraint: Subject to DFARS, FAR, and U.S. government contracting compliance, including TINA/certified cost-or-pricing data rules and CAS. Any pricing adjustment or claim must be fully compliant and documented.

Strategic constraint: Cannot walk away from strategic programs. Several FFP contracts are tied to flagship platforms central to customer relationships and future award eligibility; abandonment would forfeit positioning and incur termination liability.

Competitive constraint: High recompete risk. An aggressive pricing posture or perceived non-performance jeopardizes follow-on awards and re-compete outcomes on multi-billion-dollar program franchises.

Quality/safety constraint: Defense and flight-critical work is governed by AS9100, customer source inspection, and airworthiness requirements. Labor and material reductions cannot compromise quality, safety, or first-article conformance.
Capital/financial constraint: Investment-grade balance sheet must be preserved; major restructuring or write-downs would signal program distress to customers and investors.

businessProblem: A mid-cap aerospace & defense contractor with $2.1B revenue has seen EBITDA margin compress 200 basis points in one year (10.0% to 8.0%, EBITDA $204M to $168M) despite revenue growth and a strong $5.6B backlog (2.7x revenue, book-to-bill 1.1). Input costs have surged: materials +12% (to $735M, 35% of revenue) and labor +8% (to $546M, 26% of revenue). The structural issue is that approximately 70% of revenue ($1,470M) is concentrated in firm-fixed-price multi-year government and prime contracts that were priced before the inflation surge and that lack economic price adjustment (EPA) clauses. On this book, input-cost inflation cannot be passed through, while only the ~30% cost-plus/escalating book ($630M) recovers cost increases. Demand is strong and the backlog is full, so this is not a demand, volume, or market-share problem, and operational efficiency is not the identified gap. The central question is whether the margin decline is a structural pricing/contracting problem, a unit-economics/operations problem, or an operational bottleneck. The CEO must decide, within ~120 days, how to price next-cycle FFP bids and whether to file Requests for Equitable Adjustment (REAs) on existing contracts before the re-pricing window closes and before bidding additional FFP work that could lock in further underpriced backlog.

evidence.finding: EBITDA margin declined 200 bps from 10.0% (FY2024) to 8.0% (FY2025), with EBITDA falling from $204M to $168M (-$36M) even though revenue grew from $2,040M to $2,100M (+2.9%). Margin contracted while volume rose, indicating a profitability-per-dollar problem rather than a demand problem. Applying the FY2024 margin to FY2025 revenue would have implied ~$210M EBITDA, versus $168M actual, a ~$42M margin drag.
evidence.source: SEC 10-K income statement and segment disclosures (FY2024, FY2025); MD&A margin bridge

evidence.finding: Approximately 70% of revenue ($1,470M) is firm-fixed-price (FFP) multi-year contracts without economic price adjustment (EPA) clauses; only ~30% ($630M) is cost-plus or carries escalation. On the FFP book, input-cost inflation cannot be passed through to the customer, so all material and labor inflation on that revenue compresses margin directly. The ~30% cost-reimbursable/escalating book recovers most cost increases, concentrating the entire inflation impact on the FFP portfolio.
evidence.source: SEC 10-K contract-type / segment disclosures and remaining performance obligation schedules

evidence.finding: Materials cost rose to $735M (35% of revenue) up +12% YoY like-for-like, and direct labor rose to $546M (26% of revenue) up +8% YoY. The increases are input-price driven (commodity and wage inflation), not efficiency-driven: there is no disclosed deterioration in productivity, scrap, rework, or throughput. The cost increase is being absorbed because contract prices on the FFP book are fixed, not because operations became less efficient.
evidence.source: SEC 10-K cost-of-sales schedules; MD&A inflation and wage commentary

evidence.finding: Backlog stands at $5.6B (2.7x annual revenue) with book-to-bill of 1.1, indicating strong, growing demand and a deep book of future-period work. The company is not losing orders or market share; on the contrary, it continues to win work. This rules out a demand-shortfall or market-decline explanation and indicates the locked backlog itself carries the embedded pricing exposure: future periods will recognize revenue at pre-inflation fixed prices on the FFP portion of backlog.
evidence.source: SEC 10-K backlog and book-to-bill disclosures; investor presentation order metrics

evidence.finding: Estimating the inflation impact attributable to the FFP book: of the $735M materials cost, ~70% ($514.5M) supports FFP revenue; the embedded +12% inflation on that base is ~$61.7M. Of the $546M labor, ~70% ($382.2M) supports FFP revenue; the embedded +8% inflation is ~$30.6M. Combined, ~$92M of input inflation is attributable to the no-EPA FFP book and is structurally unrecoverable through pricing. Net realized EBITDA drag (~$42M) is smaller than gross inflation because the ~30% cost-plus/escalating book recovers its share and revenue growth provides partial absorption, but the unrecovered FFP inflation is the dominant driver of the 200 bps compression.
